title: AppleJeus
summary: AppleJeus is a North Korea linked campaign, also tracked as Gleaming Pisces, Citrine Sleet, UNC1720 and UNC4736, that targets cryptocurrency exchanges, trading firms and their employees. Public reporting describes a supply chain approach: the operators present themselves as a legitimate trading or software company, publish convincing product websites, and persuade victims to install a trojanised trading application. Earlier Windows installers abused a legitimate updater to sideload a malicious library, and later activity added macOS and Linux variants, fake job offers and cryptocurrency wallet or browser components delivered through social engineering. A 2024 supply chain compromise of legitimate software was also linked to this cluster in reporting. Evidence sits in installer and update logs, abnormal child processes, outbound connections from workstations, and the domains used by the fake companies. Attribution to North Korean activity comes from campaign infrastructure and tool overlap and is described with moderate confidence in public reporting.

beginner.definition: AppleJeus is a spying and theft campaign that hides inside software that looks real. Public reports link it to North Korea. Experts also call it Gleaming Pisces, Citrine Sleet and other names. The main target is money held as cryptocurrency.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attackers do not break in. They are invited in, because people install what looks like a normal trading program. Stolen cryptocurrency is very hard to get back, and there is no bank to call. A single infected laptop can lead to a stolen wallet. Checking where software comes from is a real defence, not a paperwork exercise.
howItWorks: They create a fake company with a polished website and helpful staff.
They offer a trading or price program that looks useful and professional.
You download and install it, and a hidden part comes with it.
The hidden part contacts their server and waits for orders.
They watch your activity and look for wallets, keys and accounts.
They move the funds out, often in many small quick transfers.
beginner.example: Imagine a pop up shop that sells excellent cheap watches. The watches work, and word spreads. But each box also carries a copy of the shop's key, so the owner can visit your flat at night. The product was real; the friendly shop was the trap.
takeaways: Download trading and wallet software only from the official source.
Keep large crypto holdings in cold storage, away from daily computers.
A fake company can look completely professional, so verify before you install.

objectives: Explain how trojanised software turns installation into an intrusion.
Describe supply chain risk when legitimate software or updaters are abused.
Identify the endpoint and network artifacts left by a trojanised trading application.
List protective controls for cryptocurrency holdings used by an organisation.
State what is known and uncertain about public attribution of this campaign.
